title: Louis Rossmann Wants More People to Care About the Right to Repair
gist: Brian Barrett's Wired Big Interview with Louis Rossmann frames right to repair as one piece of a broader fight over ownership: subscriptions, server-tethered devices and post-sale firmware changes, all shielded by DMCA Section 1201. Rossmann argues corporate repair programs are superficial, that AI coding tools like Claude Code can break digital locks but may be curbed by their providers, and that local models will eventually free users; he is pushing durable 1201 repair legislation after Democrats won both chambers in the midterms.

insights.claim: Louis Rossmann argues the core problem is not just repairability but the erosion of ownership: products turning into subscriptions and requiring a connection to the manufacturer's server, which lets companies disable them at any time.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Device-as-a-service and connected-hardware business models carry growing regulatory and reputational risk.
insights.quote: everything is turning into a subscription, that the things that you buy must connect to the manufacturer’s server in order to work
insights.locator: As time went on, my channel stopped

insights.claim: A thermostat company pushed a firmware update after going bankrupt that required owners to pay $117 a year to regain functionality they previously had.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Post-sale paywalling of existing features is the type of practice most likely to trigger consumer-protection action.
insights.locator: Some of my favorites are some of these thermostat companies

insights.claim: Amazon has removed Kindle books from devices after purchase because buyers hold only an end-user license, not ownership, illustrating how copyrightable software undermines digital ownership.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Licensing-not-owning remains a latent consumer backlash risk for digital-content platforms.
insights.locator: I think people are now waking up to this

insights.claim: Apple's self-repair program requires renting nearly 80 pounds of equipment and using official parts, saving little versus the Apple Store, and third-party screens or cameras can trigger feature lockouts via parts recognition.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Parts-pairing keeps repair revenue captive despite nominal self-repair concessions; a target for legislation.
insights.locator: Apple did start offering self-repair services

insights.claim: Samsung's independent repair program sold batteries only glued to the screen as a combined part costing over $200, which Rossmann says makes it useless for phones worth about $200.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Corporate 'pro-repair' announcements can be economically hollow; scrutinize part pricing, not headlines.
insights.locator: One of the examples I have of this is with Samsung

insights.claim: Rossmann says right-to-repair gains so far are mostly cultural, plus memorandums of understanding with companies, rather than legislative, and farmers still use cracked Ukrainian software to repair John Deere tractors without dealers.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: John Deere's dealer-service lock-in remains intact in practice despite publicized concessions.
insights.quote: They’re still using cracked Ukrainian software to be able to work on their tractor themselves
insights.locator: I think a lot of the change so far

insights.claim: Rossmann's core repair ask is the ability to buy the same parts manufacturers use; he says chip distributors refuse to sell to unlisted buyers and Apple tells chipmakers not to sell to independent repairers.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Parts-supply restrictions are the choke point; legislation targeting parts access would hit OEM service margins.
insights.quote: Apple tells the company that makes this chip not to sell it to me
insights.locator: I like to tell them

insights.claim: Rossmann rebuts manufacturers' quality-control justification for restricting unauthorized parts by noting his shop has a better Google Maps rating than every Apple Store in the US.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Quality-control arguments for repair restrictions are weakening in public debate.
insights.quote: why does my store have a better rating on Google Maps than every single Apple Store in the country?
insights.locator: If the issue is quality control

insights.claim: People are using Claude Code to strip bloatware and adware from smart TVs and even to remake Adobe Suite, and Rossmann sees AI as a powerful tool for breaking digital locks.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: AI coding agents lower the cost of circumventing vendor software control, pressuring ad- and lock-in-driven device models.
insights.quote: I love the idea of it being used to break digital locks
insights.locator: I love it. I love seeing people

insights.claim: Rossmann predicts frontier AI providers may eventually be pressured by companies to block uses like freeing users from vendor lock-in, and that within one to two years tools like Claude Code might detect and refuse attempts to escape Adobe.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Cloud-hosted AI's guardrails could become a corporate-protection layer, boosting demand for local models.
insights.locator: You know, when people are remaking Adobe Suite

insights.claim: Rossmann expects local AI models running on standard laptops, including models from countries outside the US, to eventually let users bypass digital locks without permission from AI companies, though not within the next year or two.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis for capable local/edge models as a user-sovereignty play.
insights.locator: But what I’m hoping to see happen

insights.claim: DMCA Section 1201 makes it illegal to bypass a technical protection measure to access a protected work even for repair, and Rossmann says its architect Bruce Lehman routed it through an international treaty to sidestep Congress's rejection.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Section 1201 is the legal backbone of device lock-in; its reform is the key regulatory variable.
insights.locator: Section 1201 of the DMCA makes it illegal

insights.claim: Rossmann says Section 1201 failed at its anti-piracy purpose, which its architect admitted in 2007 and 2013, while burdening law-abiding users who want to use media and devices they bought.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Weak anti-piracy justification strengthens the case for repair exemptions becoming permanent law.
insights.quote: These laws fundamentally have not worked
insights.locator: The architect of the law also said

insights.claim: Rather than seeking annual Section 1201 exemptions, right-to-repair advocates aim to pass durable legislation, starting with making repair of owned products not a crime.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: A narrow repair-only carve-out is the most likely first legislative step.
insights.locator: Instead of every single year going back

insights.claim: After Democrats won control of the Senate and House in the midterms, right-to-repair supporters such as Josh Turek in Iowa and likely Jake Johnson in Minnesota are entering Congress, but Rossmann expects the issue to compete with many other priorities.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Raises odds of right-to-repair legislation modestly in the next Congress; watch for bills on 1201.
insights.locator: So we’re talking not long after the midterms

insights.claim: Rossmann says Biden's summer 2021 executive order including right to repair produced little concrete result.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Executive actions have had limited impact; durable change requires legislation.
insights.locator: So I am happy to see that there are people

insights.claim: Rossmann's FULU organization ran the 'Own Your Shit' tour across 13 US cities to build voter pressure on Congress, featuring a former FTC commissioner in San Jose.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Grassroots mobilization is aimed at making right to repair an electoral issue.
insights.locator: And that’s part of what we’ve been trying

insights.claim: FULU pays bounties to people who restore functionality disabled by digital locks; a $5,000 bounty for a bricked Futurehome thermostat was claimed by an employee who built a Home Assistant integration restoring it.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Bounties create a counterforce to post-sale feature removal, raising reputational cost for OEMs.
insights.locator: I said, “5,000 bucks to whoever makes this work again.”

insights.claim: Rossmann argues the movement grows by tangible personal wins, such as a repair costing $200 versus Apple's $2,000 quote, rather than abstract lecturing.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Consumer savings stories drive adoption of independent repair, eroding OEM service revenue.
insights.locator: I try to avoid talking about it

insights.claim: Rossmann says right to repair has been a 12-year slow burn rather than a single inflection, citing a 2018 CBC News piece where Apple quoted a motherboard repair that he fixed by bending back a single pin.
insights.speaker: Brian Barrett
insights.so_what: Media exposure of OEM repair overquoting is a persistent reputational risk for Apple.
insights.locator: I think it’s been a slow burn
